{{Short description|Mathematical model of abstract computation}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2026}}
{{turing}}
In his book ''[[A New Kind of Science]]'', [[Stephen Wolfram]] described a [[Universal Turing machine|universal]] 2-state 5-symbol [[Turing machine]], and conjectured that a particular '''2-state 3-symbol Turing machine''' (hereinafter '''(2,3) Turing machine''') might be universal as well.<ref>{{cite book | last=Wolfram | first=Stephen | author-link=Stephen Wolfram | year=2002 | title=A New Kind of Science | page=709 | url=http://www.wolframscience.com/nksonline/page-709 | access-date=2009-02-10 }}</ref>

On 14 May 2007, Wolfram announced a $25,000 prize to be won by the first person to prove or disprove the universality of the (2,3) Turing machine.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Wolfram 2,3 Turing Machine Research Prize | url=http://www.wolframscience.com/prizes/tm23/ | access-date=2009-02-10 }}</ref> On 24 October 2007, it was announced that the prize had been won by Alex Smith, a student in electronics and computing at the [[University of Birmingham]], for his proof that it was "universal". Since the proof applies to a non-standard Turing machine model which allows infinite, non-periodic initial configurations and never halts it is categorized by some as "weak-universal".<ref>{{Citation|last=Goodman-Strauss|first=Chaim|title=Can't decide? Undecide!|url=http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.164.306|access-date=2022-02-04|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220205095610/http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.164.306|archive-date=5 February 2022}}</ref>

==Background==
{{See also|Universal Turing machine#Smallest machines}}
[[Claude Shannon]] first explicitly posed the question of finding the smallest possible universal Turing machine in 1956. He showed that two symbols were sufficient so long as enough states were used (or vice versa), and that it was always possible to exchange states for symbols.

Minsky (1967) briefly argued that standard (2,2) machines cannot be universal and M. Margenstern (2010) provided a [[mathematical proof]]<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.complex-systems.com/abstracts/v19_i01_a02.html | title=Turing Machines with Two Letters and Two States | work=[[Complex Systems (journal)|Complex Systems]] | year=2010 | access-date=2017-10-25 }}</ref> based on a result by L. Pavlotskaya in 1973 (not published but mentioned in Margenstern article). These proofs apply to normal Turing machine models in which the machine is given a finite input and must halt when it completes. Wolfram's machine does not satisfy either of these constraints.

There are a number of common variations of Turing machine models commonly used by computer scientists. These variations commonly include number of tapes, whether the tape(s) are two-way infinite or only one-way infinite, whether the machine head is allowed to stay put, or must move after each transition, whether or not a TM instruction can both move the head and write a symbol on the same step, etc. For each such model, there will be a different "smallest possible universal Turing machine". So, Wolfram's machine is only the "smallest possible universal Turing machine" for its (particularly nonstandard) model.

== Description ==

The following table indicates the actions to be performed by the Turing machine depending on whether its current state is '''A''' or '''B''', and the symbol currently being read is 0, 1 or 2. The table entries indicate the symbol to be printed, the direction in which the tape head is to move, and the subsequent state of the machine.

:{| class="wikitable"
! style="width:20px;"| !! A !! B
|-
! 0
| P1,R,'''B''' || P2,L,'''A'''
|-
! 1
| P2,L,'''A'''  || P2,R,'''B'''
|-
! 2
| P1,L,'''A'''  || P0,R,'''A'''
|}

The (2,3) Turing machine:
*Has no halt state;
*Is trivially related to 23 other machines by interchange of states, symbols and directions.

[[File:2-state 3-symbol Turing Machine.png|location: left]]

The state of the head (up or down droplet (A and B respectively)) and the pattern of color (white, yellow and orange (0,1, and 2 respectively)) in a given row depends solely on the content of the row immediately above it.

Even though the machine has a head with only two states, and a tape that can hold only three colors (depending on the initial content of the tape), the machine's output can still be arbitrarily complex.<ref>{{cite journal| url=http://www.nature.com/news/2007/071024/full/news.2007.190.html | title=Student snags maths prize | journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | year=2007 | doi=10.1038/news.2007.190 | access-date=2009-02-10 | last1=Brumfiel | first1=Geoff | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Proof of universality==
On 24 October 2007, it was announced by [[Wolfram Research]] that Alex Smith, a student in electronics and computing at the [[University of Birmingham]] (UK), proved that the (2,3) Turing machine is universal and thus won Wolfram's prize described above.<ref>{{cite magazine| url=http://blog.wired.com/wiredscience/2007/10/college-kid-pro.html | title=College Kid Proves That Wolfram's Turing Machine is the Simplest Universal Computer | access-date=2009-02-10 | magazine=Wired | first=Brandon | last=Keim | date=2007-10-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Geoff Brumfiel |url=http://www.nature.com/news/2007/071024/full/news.2007.190.html |title=Nature.com |journal=Nature |publisher=Nature.com |date= 24 October 2007|doi=10.1038/news.2007.190 |access-date=2010-03-09|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn12826-simplest-universal-computer-wins-student-25000.html |title=Simplest 'universal computer' wins student $25,000 |publisher=New Scientist |access-date=2010-03-09 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251121104746/https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn12826-simplest-universal-computer-wins-student-25000/ |archive-date=21 November 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.newscentre.bham.ac.uk/press/2007/10/24Oct07Turingprize.shtml |title=U of Birmingham |publisher=Newscentre.bham.ac.uk |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ams.org/mathmedia/mathdigest/md-200710-toc.html |title=Math in the news from Math Society |publisher=Ams.org |access-date=2010-03-09 |archive-date=20 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100220060553/http://www.ams.org/mathmedia/mathdigest/md-200710-toc.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Crighton |first=Ben |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/more_or_less/7112637.stm |title= Proving Turing's simple computer|publisher=BBC News |date=2007-11-26 |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bitwisemag.com/2/Did-Computers-Just-Get-Simpler |title=Bitwise Mag article |publisher=Bitwise Mag article |date=2007-10-24 |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.maa.org/devlin/devlin_11_07.html |title=Mathematical Association of America |publisher=Maa.org |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article.cfm?id=simplest-computer-new-kind-science |title=A New Kind of Science Author Pays Brainy Undergrad $25,000 for Identifying Simplest Computer | first=J. R. | last=Minkel | journal=[[Scientific American]] |date=2007-10-25 |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://plus.maths.org/latestnews/sep-dec07/turing/index.html |title=plus magazine |publisher=Plus.maths.org |date=8 November 2007 |access-date=2010-03-09 |archive-date=20 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091220205222/http://plus.maths.org/latestnews/sep-dec07/turing/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2007/nov/29/research |title=Complex proof of a very simple computer | first=Tom | last=Stuart | newspaper=The Guardian |date=2007-11-29|access-date=2010-03-09 | location=London}}</ref>

The proof showed that the machine is equivalent to a variant of a [[tag system]] already known to be universal. Smith first constructed a sequence of rule systems showing that the (2,3) Turing machine is capable of arbitrary finite computations. He then employed a novel approach to extend that construction to unbounded computations. The proof proceeds in two stages. The first part emulates the finite evolution of any two-color cyclic tag system. The emulation is a composite of a series of emulations involving the indexed rule systems 'system 0' through 'system 5'. Each rule system emulates the next one in the sequence. Smith then showed that even though the initial condition of the (2,3) Turing machine is not repetitive, the construction of that initial condition is not universal. Hence the (2,3) Turing machine is universal.

Wolfram claims that Smith's proof is another piece of evidence for Wolfram's general "Principle of Computational Equivalence" (PCE).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-October/012149.html|title=Stephen Wolfram reply in the FOM list | publisher=[[New York University]] | date=October 2007 }}</ref> That principle states that if one sees behavior that is not obviously simple, the behavior will correspond to a computation that is in a sense "maximally sophisticated".<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.ddj.com/blog/portal/archives/2007/05/the_prize_and_u.html | title=The Wolfram Prize and Universal Computation: It's Your Problem Now}}</ref> Smith's proof has unleashed a debate on the precise operational conditions a Turing machine must satisfy in order for it to be candidate universal machine.

A universal (2,3) Turing machine has conceivable applications.<ref>{{cite journal| url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn12826-simplest-universal-computer-wins-student-25000.html | title=Simplest 'universal computer' wins student $25,000 | journal=[[New Scientist]] | date=24 October 2007 | access-date=28 January 2016 }}</ref> For instance, a machine that small and simple can be embedded or constructed using a small number of particles or molecules. But the "compiler" Smith's algorithm implies does not produce compact or efficient code, at least for anything but the simplest cases. Hence the resulting code tends to be astronomically large and very inefficient. Whether there exist more efficient codings enabling the (2,3) Turing machine to compute more rapidly is an open question.

===Dispute===
The announcement that Alex Smith's proof had won was made without the approval of the judging committee,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-October/012163.html |title=[FOM&#93; Smallest universal machine |publisher=Cs.nyu.edu |date= 30 October 2007|access-date=2022-08-18}}</ref> as noted by [[Martin Davis (mathematician)|Martin Davis]], a member of the committee, in a post to the [[FOM mailing list]]:

: "As far as I know, no member of the committee has passed on the validity of this 40 page proof. The determination that Smith's proof is correct seems to have been made entirely by the Wolfram organization. My understanding is that the I/O involves complex encodings."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-October/012132.html |title=[FOM&#93; Smallest universal machine |publisher=Cs.nyu.edu |date= 26 October 2007|access-date=2022-08-18}}</ref>

[[Vaughan Pratt]] subsequently disputed the correctness of this proof in a post to the mailing list,<ref>{{cite web | url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-October/012156.html | title=Vaughan Pratt's message to the FOM list| date=29 October 2007}}</ref> noting that similar techniques would allow a [[linear bounded automaton]] (or LBA) to be universal, which would contradict a known non-universality result due to [[Noam Chomsky]]. Alex Smith joined the mailing list after this message and replied on the following day explaining that an LBA would require to be restarted manually to become universal using the same initial configuration, while his construction restarts the Turing machine automatically with no external intervention.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-October/012164.html|title=Alex Smith's first reply to Vaughan Pratt in the FOM list|date=30 October 2007 }}</ref> Discussions about the proof continued for some time between Alex Smith, Vaughan Pratt, and others.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2007-November/thread.html |title=FOM list archive for November 2007 |publisher=Cs.nyu.edu |access-date=2010-03-09}}</ref>

===Publication===
Smith's proof was finally published in Wolfram's journal [[Complex Systems (journal)|''Complex Systems'']] in 2020.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Smith | first=Alex | date=2020 | title=Universality of Wolfram's 2, 3 Turing Machine | journal=Complex Systems | volume=29 | issue=1 | pages=1–44 | doi=10.25088/ComplexSystems.29.1.1| s2cid=17142621 }}</ref>
